scenes.title: A needle that flips

sentences.text: This needle has pointed north your whole life.
But the seafloor remembers further back.
North and south have swapped.
Again and again, with no schedule.

scenes.visual: Render class webgl. NIGHT background, no hand (G3). A stylized 3D compass in macro, seen from about 30 degrees above: matte grey body, white dial ticks, the letters N and S, needle with a vermillion (--b) north tip and a grey tail; soft rim light, slow 5 % camera push-in over the whole scene. Lead-in (1.0 s, no voice): the needle swings in from east and settles on north with Kit.needle (corner: false) and Scene.spring, at most 3 % overshoot; a faint idle wobble afterwards so the frame is never still. This is the birth of motif M1. On 'remember': the reference lower-third (kind 'reference', bottom-left) 'Reference' / 'Vine & Matthews 1963 · seafloor stripes', 3 s. On 'flip-0.15' (lands at about 7 s, BRIEF D20): the needle swings 180 degrees round to south in 1.0 s and holds; with it the plain chip 'illustration, not to time scale' fades in centred under the compass (y about 820) and stays to the end; two-note needle sound (sfx). On 'again': two translucent ghost needles (30 % opacity) sweep south-north-south in quick succession behind the real needle, 0.5 s each, to suggest repetition without a clock; then the solid needle settles back on north at 'again+0.6'. Badge CONTEXT top-right from 'north'. Hard cut is not used: the compass stays centred and becomes the first layer of the 00.2 zoom.

scenes.title: Pull back to the planet

sentences.text: That needle follows a {b}field{/} that wraps the whole planet.
It feels permanent.
It is not.

chips: REFERENCE · NOAA NCEI · close to a dipole field

scenes.visual: Render class flat for the zoom; only the final sphere (about 3 s) is WebGL, rendered as a separate shot and cut in on 'permanent' (G4). Transition T2 scale dive, in reverse. Lead-in: the 00.1 compass, same framing. On 'planet-0.15': a 'Powers of Ten' pull-back made of flat layered illustrations cross-faded on a log scale, 3.5 s in all: compass on a tabletop, the room, a coastline landscape, a cloud layer, then the whole Earth as a matte grey sphere (matter is grey: no blue ocean, blue means velocity). On 'permanent': vermillion dipole field lines bloom from one pole to the other around the sphere, their axis tilted about 9.4 degrees from the spin axis (params.dipole_tilt_deg; NOAA gives 9.41 degrees today, 'about 11' is the older textbook value; the angle is not labelled), arrowheads showing direction; the lines breathe slowly (idle motion). On 'not': the field lines thin and dim to half strength for 0.5 s and recover, a single flicker that hints at change; then the camera starts to dive toward one ocean (T2) so that 00.3 opens on the ridge. Chip SCHEMATIC (grey dashed, bottom-right, from 'planet'); reference lower-third from 'permanent': 'Reference' / 'NOAA NCEI · close to a dipole field'. Badge CONTEXT top-right.

scenes.title: The seafloor tape recorder

params.polarity_source: Cande and Kent 1995, as tabulated in the composite GPTS of Gee and Kent 2007 (Tauxe, Essentials of Paleomagnetism, Table 15.1)

sentences.text: At ocean ridges, fresh lava cools into rock.
Tiny magnetic grains lock in the {b}field's{/} direction.
The seafloor spreads, and each flip starts a new stripe.
Five million years, about twenty flips, and wildly uneven gaps.

labels: about 20 flips in 5 million years · no schedule
chips: REFERENCE · Vine & Matthews 1963 · polarity ages: Cande & Kent 1995

scenes.visual: Render class flat. Opens from the 00.2 dive. On 'ridge': cross-section of a mid-ocean ridge, ridge axis at the centre: dark water band (near-background grey, never blue), grey crust, a light-grey glowing magma column rising in the axis and cooling to mid-grey rock (no key colour for magma: vermillion is the field, amber is metrics). Label 'ridge'. On 'grains': zoom on the axis; above it a vermillion field arrow (pointing north = normal); about a dozen short grain ticks in the newly formed rock rotate to line up with the arrow, then stop moving as the rock solidifies; label 'new rock'. On 'spread': zoom out; two conveyor belts carry the crust left and right; time runs from 5 million years ago to today in about 4.5 s, driven by params.normal_Ma at a constant schematic spreading rate (as in the USGS model profile): at each polarity boundary the field arrow flips 180 degrees and the rock forming at the axis switches state, so stripes accumulate mirror-symmetrically on both sides as a true barcode (A5): solid vermillion = normal, near-background (--b-neg, darkest shade) = reversed, labels 'normal' and 'reversed' kept; the widest stripe, today's, is at the axis. Chip SCHEMATIC (grey dashed) on the cross-section. On 'uneven': the camera tilts down to a top view of the right-hand barcode; it slides left and morphs (T1) into the film's horizontal polarity strip (Kit.barcode, series built from params.normal_Ma: +1 in normal intervals, -1 in reversed ones, 0.01 Myr linear ramps at the boundaries) with a time axis 'millions of years ago' 5 4 3 2 1 0 (today on the right); a thin vermillion step trace above the strip shows the sign only (labels 'north' and 'south', no amplitude, no symbol D, so no corner needle); caption 'about 20 flips in 5 million years · no schedule' (amber is not used: this is a record, not a metric). The SCHEMATIC chip is replaced on 'uneven' by the reference lower-third 'Reference' / 'Vine & Matthews 1963 · polarity ages: Cande & Kent 1995'. The two 10 000-year subchrons (1.201-1.211 and 2.140-2.150 Ma) must stay visible as thin lines (at least 2 px). Badge CONTEXT top-right.

scenes.title: Two questions

sentences.text: So, two questions.
When will it flip next?
And {metric}how often{/} does it flip?
Which one can we answer?
In a simple computer model of a flipping {b}field{/}, the first is hopeless.
The second is not.
Finding out why takes us through liquid metal and chaos.
Then to {model}machines{/} that dream up snapshots of {b}magnetic fields{/}.
They must obey some laws exactly, and others only on average.

chips: for Earth: no one can say if or when · NOAA NCEI

scenes.visual: Render class flat. On 'two': the polarity strip of 00.3 shrinks to a thin band along the top edge (continuity, it stays faintly there) and two cards slide in side by side, each about 700 px wide. Left card 'When will it flip next?' with a grey clock icon; right card 'How often does it flip?' with amber (--metric) tally marks: amber because the crossing rate is a distribution-level quantity. On 'when': the left card lights and the clock hands sweep once; a small reference chip under it, 'for Earth: no one can say if or when · NOAA NCEI', so that the next sentence is heard as a statement about a model, not about Earth. On 'often': the right card lights; four amber tally marks are drawn one after the other with a soft tick each (page events, tick at about -30 dB). On 'bet' (predict beat, hold 1.5 s from the script): both cards pulse once and then only breathe; nothing new appears during the hold. On 'hopeless-0.15': the plain chip 'three-mode model (Gissinger 2012)' appears on the clock card, then its border turns dashed, its hands spin into a blur and the card dims to 40 %; formula layer item 1 (Lyapunov time against the mean time between zero crossings). On 'answer': the tally card stays lit and the pen (M9) underlines 'How often'; formula layer item 2 (Rice), label 'Formula · R:514'. On 'path': under the cards a small roadmap row is drawn left to right, three grey line icons: the compass needle (vermillion tip), a tank of liquid metal, a chaotic two-lobed curve. On 'dream-0.15': the violet cloud teaser (M4, Kit.cloud, 3 s, the film's second protagonist, A6): a seeded round Gaussian of violet points flows along about 60 straight strings onto the two-lobed cloud of real generated snapshots: data cloud, variants.C_equivariant.x, first params.cloud_points rows, columns D (horizontal) and Q (vertical), range params.cloud_range, no axes; violet chip 'generated snapshots · E1 three-mode model' (no Γ in a chip at L0) and the source lower-third filled from the file's meta.stamp (provenance stamp, small mono type); granular hiss (sfx). No corner needle in this scene: D is never labelled on screen outside the formula layer. On 'exact': two small tags appear under the cloud, 'exact' in a solid outline and 'on average' in a dashed outline (a first glimpse of the two shelves of 07.1 and 08.6). At most three key colours at once (amber, violet, vermillion). Badge MEASURED top-right with the note params.badge_note ('three-mode model'): the claim is shown for that model only (Lyapunov time about 11 against more than 100 between crossings; Rice recovers the crossing rate from snapshots plus the equations, 4 to 6 % cumulative error on the reference distribution in E1).

question.en: Should the first simulations target *how often* the field flips, or the warning signs *just before* a flip?
question.fr: Les premières simulations doivent-elles viser la fréquence des renversements du champ, ou les signes annonciateurs juste avant un renversement ?
question.why: Rates can come from snapshots plus the equations; warning signs need dense records around each flip, and a run holds few flips.
question.unblocks: Run length and output cadence: spaced snapshots, or dense series around each flip.
question.why_fr: Une fréquence peut se déduire d'instantanés et des équations ; des signes annonciateurs exigent des enregistrements denses autour de chaque renversement, et une simulation en contient peu.
question.unblocks_fr: Durée des simulations et cadence de sauvegarde : instantanés espacés, ou séries denses autour de chaque renversement.

scenes.title: No magnet inside

chapter.title: A planet that makes its own magnet

sentences.text: Is there a giant magnet hidden inside the Earth?
Deep down, the outer core is an ocean of liquid iron.
Left alone, a {b}field{/} there would fade away within tens of thousands of years.
Yet Earth's field is several billion years old.
So the moving iron must keep making it, all the time.

scenes.title: Lines never end

box_rests: the north end of the right half

sentences.text: Take a bar magnet: north at one end, south at the other.
Cut it in half.
You get two magnets, each with a north and a south.
No one has ever found a lone magnetic pole.
{b}Field lines{/} say the same: they never start or stop.
Draw any box, and count.
As many lines go in as come out.
Keep this box in mind.

labels: field lines never start or stop

formulas.tex: \nabla\cdot\B = 0 \iff \oint_{\partial V}\B\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = 0\ \text{ for every closed surface } \partial V

chips: REFERENCE · Univ. of Illinois Physics Van 2008 · cutting a magnet
REFERENCE · no isolated magnetic pole ever observed · P1 §3.3

scenes.visual: Render class dense2d. On 'cut': the pen (M9) draws a chalk cut line across the middle; the halves slide apart by 160 px each (1.0 s, cubic). On 'two-0.15': new letters pop at the cut faces (the left half's cut face becomes N, the right half's becomes S) and the field lines re-form around two separate magnets (two precomputed line sets, 0.8 s cross-fade inside the scene); soft pop (sfx); reference lower-third 'Reference' / 'Univ. of Illinois Physics Van 2008 · cutting a magnet', 4 s. On 'never': above the magnets a ghost 'lone pole' (a small grey dot labelled 'N alone' with straight lines radiating out, 35 % opacity, redrawn after the left panel of P1's figure fig-monopole-dipole; the PNG itself is not shown, its white ground would flash on NIGHT) appears and the pen draws a cross over it; plain chip 'no isolated magnetic pole ever observed · P1 §3.3' under it. scenes.title: The squeal

params.note: illustrative ratios only: no number of these is ever shown on screen (SCHEMATIC)

sentences.text: A bicycle dynamo turns motion into electricity, using a built-in magnet.
The Earth has to make its own. The trick: a loop.
Hold a microphone near its own speaker, and turn up the {param}gain{/}.
Below a certain point, a whisper fades.
Past it, the loop feeds itself.
Now spin a copper disc wired to a coil around its axle.
Current makes {b}field{/}, and field makes current.
Spin it faster and faster. Does the field grow bit by bit, or not at all until some speed?
Not at all, until a threshold.
Past it, each turn multiplies a tiny {b}seed field{/} by the same factor: exponential growth.
Just past the threshold, growth is slow.
Then the field brakes the disc, and growth stops.

labels: Does the field grow bit by bit, or not at all until some speed?

formulas.tex: L_c\,\dot I + R_c\,I = \frac{\cp{\Omega}\,M}{2\pi}\,I \;\Rightarrow\; I \propto e^{s t},\qquad s = \Big(\frac{\cp{\Omega}\,M}{2\pi} - R_c\Big)\Big/ L_c

chips: REFERENCE · bicycle generator with a permanent magnet · Chiu 2004, US patent 6,703,716

scenes.title: Frozen threads

params.note: schematic tuning values (pixels, scene seconds), not physical data; the two panels differ only by kappa

sentences.text: What kind of motion can grow a {b}magnetic field{/}?
In a perfect conductor, field lines would be threads frozen into the fluid.
Wherever the {u}flow{/} stretches a thread, the field along it grows stronger.
Real metals let the threads smudge, like spreading ink.
The smudging speed is set by the metal's {param}magnetic diffusivity{/}.
Same flow, two metals.
A good conductor smudges slowly: the threads stay sharp.
A poor one smudges fast: the threads blur away.

onscreen.title: Stretch, smudge, and three tanks of sodium

Small Rm: smudging wins.

At low Rm, the seed dies away.
Past a threshold, the growth rate crosses zero and the seed grows, like the squeal.

scenes.title: The sodium problem

sentences.text: Laboratory dynamos use liquid sodium.
It flows as easily as water.
But a field smudges in it about a hundred thousand times faster than its swirls do.
Their ratio, one in a hundred thousand, is the {param}magnetic Prandtl number{/}, Pm.
Reaching an Rm of a few tens takes violent stirring.
The flow's {param}Reynolds number{/}, the gauge of turbulence, reaches millions.
So every laboratory dynamo is turbulent.

labels: field smudges about 100 000 × faster than swirls
chips: REFERENCE · Nore et al. 2018 · sodium at 120 °C

scenes.visual: Render class flat. On 'sodium': a grey tank of liquid metal in cutaway (matter grey --matter, a silvery surface line), label 'liquid sodium' (no temperature on the tank: params.sodium_temperature_C = 120 °C is the VKS working temperature of Nore et al. 2018, not that of every experiment, Riga first ran at 205 °C, so it appears only on the formula layer). On 'water': the tank tilts and pours; two streams side by side, 'sodium' (mid grey) and 'water' (light grey; matter is grey, water is NOT blue: blue means velocity), same width, same speed, same splash (identical spline animations); label 'about as runny as water'; formula layer item 1. On 'fast': the pours clear; two soft blobs side by side start to spread by diffusion at the same moment: a blue swirl (a small vortex of rotating blue streaks: the flow) and a vermillion field blob; the vermillion blob spreads and fades within about 1 s while the blue swirl has barely widened by the end of the scene (visually static: its spreading is about 100 000 times slower); label 'field smudges about 100 000 × faster than swirls'. On 'pm': the green ratio params.pm_label appears between the blobs, nu under the blue swirl with the words 'swirl smudging' and eta under the vermillion blob with 'field smudging'; the reference lower-third 'Reference' / 'Nore et al. 2018 · sodium at 120 °C' for 4 s; formula layer item 2. On 'stir': the blobs slide away; two round dials side by side (about 300 px each), BOTH GREEN because both are control parameters in the colour key (the outline said 'Re blue'; the flow itself is the blue texture): left 'Rm' on a linear dial params.rm_dial with the window params.rm_window shaded green at 12 %; right 'Re, Reynolds number' on a log dial with ticks 10³ to 10⁷ (params.re_dial_log10). A grey motor icon under them spins up; the two needles move together, linked by Re = Rm / Pm with Pm = params.pm_value: as the Rm needle creeps into the window (to params.rm_needle_end), the Re needle races past 10⁶ (Scene.spring on both, at most 3 % overshoot). Behind the dials a blue turbulent texture builds up (Canvas 2D advected noise, G5: no full-screen shader), its opacity tied to the Re needle, at most params.texture_max_opacity. On 're': the word 'millions' under the Re dial; formula layer item 3. On 'turbulent': the caption 'Rm ~ 10–50 needs Re ~ millions' at top centre and, under it, 'every laboratory dynamo is turbulent'; the texture at full strength to the end. No exponents in the narration (outline: level lowered to L1); the exact values live on the formula layer. Chip SCHEMATIC on the blobs and dials (pictures, not measurements). Badge CONTEXT. Key colours: green, blue, vermillion (vermillion only in the 'fast' and 'pm' beats).

scenes.title: Three tanks that worked

cards.name: RIGA
cards.line: corkscrew flow → a field that oscillates and turns

cards.name: KARLSRUHE

cards.name: VKS
cards.line: two counter-rotating impellers · 150 L of sodium · up to 300 kW → a dipole that can flip

sentences.text: Only three liquid-sodium experiments have made their own field, each a different kind.
In Riga, a corkscrew flow made a field that oscillates and slowly turns.
In Karlsruhe, fifty-two spiralling cells made a steady field, close to a {b}dipole{/}.
And only VKS, at Cadarache, made a dipole that can flip.
A fourth, DRESDYN in Dresden, aims to join them: a spinning cylinder whose axis slowly turns.

labels: corkscrew flow → a field that oscillates and turns
52 spiralling cells → a steady, dipole-like field
two counter-rotating impellers · 150 L of sodium · up to 300 kW → a dipole that can flip

scenes.visual: Render class flat. Four cards in a row on a thin grey timeline (x 96-1824; each card about 400 x 520 px, 24 px gaps; one moment per card), every word and number read from params.cards (nothing typed in the scene). On 'three': the first three cards slide in from the right, 0.25 s apart, titles only, solid grey outlines; a mono caption above them 'the only three liquid-sodium dynamos'. On 'riga': card 1 lights (the others drop to 40 %): 'RIGA · Latvia', year chip 'first dynamo: November 1999'; pictogram: a grey pipe in cutaway with a blue corkscrew arrow inside (the helical flow) and, beside it, a small vermillion arrow that turns slowly around the pipe's axis while its length oscillates (an alternating, rotating field: NOT a flip); one line 'corkscrew flow → a field that oscillates and turns'; mono footer 'Gailitis et al. 2000'. On 'karlsruhe': card 2 lights: 'KARLSRUHE · Germany', 'first dynamo: December 1999'; pictogram: a grey drum seen from above holding a grid of params.cards[1].cells = 52 small blue spiral cells (draw all 52), and one steady vermillion dipole arrow across it (idle breathing only, never flips); line '52 spiralling cells → a steady, dipole-like field'; footer 'Stieglitz & Müller 2001'. On 'vks': card 3 lights: 'VKS · CEA Cadarache', '2006 (published 2007)'; pictogram redrawn in the palette from the proportions of prep/p3-mhd-dynamo/figures/vks-en.svg: a grey horizontal cylinder, two impellers with two opposed blue rotation arrows, a vermillion axial dipole arrow that flips once at 'vks+1.4' (180 degrees, at most 3 % overshoot) with a soft two-note needle sound (sfx, -20 dB); line 'two counter-rotating impellers · 150 L of sodium · up to 300 kW → a dipole that can flip'; footer 'Monchaux et al. 2007'; a chalk pen circle (M9) around the flipping arrow: the only one that flips (critique_accuracy B3). On 'dresdyn': card 4 slides in with a DASHED grey outline, everything in it grey: 'DRESDYN · HZDR, Dresden', chip 'under way'; pictogram: a grey cylinder spinning about its own axis while that axis slowly sweeps a cone (precession), no impeller, a dashed empty circle where a field glyph would be; line 'precessing cylinder, no impeller'; footer 'Stefani et al. 2015'. End state: cards 1, 2 and 4 at 70 %, card 3 at 100 % (it grows into the 3D model of 02.5, T1). Text at least 28 px: the VKS line may wrap to three lines (Kit.fit). Badge CONTEXT. scenes.title: VKS: two impellers and an iron surprise

sentences.text: Inside VKS: a cylinder holding a hundred and fifty litres of liquid sodium.
At its ends, two bladed discs, the impellers, spin in opposite directions.
Should it matter what metal the discs are made of?
With stainless steel discs, there was no dynamo, even at full speed.
Swap in discs of soft iron, and a dipole grows along the axis.
So the threshold depends on more than Rm: materials count too.

labels: two impellers, counter-rotating · motors up to 300 kW
chips: SCHEMATIC · geometry after Monchaux et al. 2007
REFERENCE · Monchaux et al. 2007 · soft-iron impellers

scenes.visual: Render class webgl (Three.js r160 vendored, Line2 fat lines 2-4 px for field lines, matte materials, long lens about 30 degrees, slow orbit of params.orbit_deg over the whole scene, at most 15 degrees per second). T1 from 02.4: the VKS card's pictogram grows into the 3D model. On 'inside': a horizontal cylinder in cutaway (front half removed), matte grey walls (--matter), the sodium volume a faint grey fill (matter is grey, never blue), proportions from params.geometry_mm (inner diameter 412 mm, discs of radius 154.5 mm, 371 mm apart); label '150 L of liquid sodium'; chip 'SCHEMATIC · geometry after Monchaux et al. 2007'. On 'discs': two impeller discs with params.blades = 8 curved blades each, near the two ends, spin in opposite directions (one turn per params.disc_turn_s seconds, visual only); label 'two impellers, counter-rotating · motors up to 300 kW'. From 'discs+1.0' the blue flow (--u): short moving blue dashes swirling around the axis in each half, each half turning with its own disc (two cells turning opposite ways), plus the poloidal recirculation loops in the cut plane, drawn as in the site figure figures/vks panel a (same topology and arrow directions). On 'predict' (predict beat; hold 2.5 s from the script): a predict card at top left, the film's predict style with the kicker 'Predict' and the line 'Does the discs' metal matter?', UNNUMBERED (the Q1-Q8 numbering of the outline is kept); during the hold nothing new appears, the discs and the blue dashes keep moving (idle). On 'steel': the predict card leaves; the discs are tagged 'stainless steel' (light grey, faint brushed sheen); a small green speed gauge (M2) climbs to its top, 'full speed'; params.seed_decays times, a few thin faint vermillion seed lines appear along the axis and fade away (decay); tag 'stainless steel: no dynamo'; the reference lower-third 'Reference' / 'Monchaux et al. 2007 · soft-iron impellers' for 4 s. On 'iron': the discs slide out along the axis and back in, darker grey (0.8 s), tag 'soft iron'; then the vermillion axial dipole grows over about 2 s: the field lines of data/fig_vks.json (data.fieldlines[k].pts, in units of the cylinder radius, upper half-plane; mirror them below the axis and revolve the set about the axis at params.fieldline_azimuths angles) are drawn on from the axis outward, axial inside the sodium and closing outside, their brightness rising like an exponential that then levels off; tag 'soft iron: dynamo'. The hold of 1.0 s after this paragraph is a breath: nothing new appears. No corner needle (the dipole is not labelled D here). On 'more': two small green knobs appear side by side at bottom right for the rest of the scene, 'Rm' and 'material' (the narration says the threshold depends on more than Rm: same sodium and same speed, hence the same Rm, with steel and with iron; a teaser of the knob panel of 03.5; no numbers). sentences.text: Now spin the two discs at different speeds.
At some settings, the dipole flips again and again, with no schedule.
Like the compass needle at the start, but every minute or two.
Each flip itself takes only about five seconds.
Uneven stripes, like the seafloor's, but written in minutes, not millions of years.

scenes.title: The induction equation, term by term

chapter.title: The equation, the windows, and the question

sentences.text: Back to the race: the {u}flow{/} stretches the field, and diffusion smudges it.
Physicists write the very same race as a single equation.
On the left: how fast the {b}magnetic field{/} changes, at each point.
First term on the right: the flow carries the field along and stretches it, like the threads.
Second term: diffusion smudges it, at a pace set by the magnetic diffusivity.
A poor conductor smudges fast.
Stretching against smudging: the whole race, in one line.

scenes.title: A conveyor belt that does not feel its cargo

sentences.text: Picture the {u}flow{/} as a conveyor belt that does not feel its cargo.
A weak {b}field{/} rides on the imposed flow, and fades or grows exponentially.
On a log scale: a straight line, whose slope is the growth rate.
But a strong field pushes back on the flow, as it braked the copper disc: the line bends into a plateau.
These are the kinematic and dynamic regimes.
Flips live on the plateau.

labels: the field pushes back on the flow

formulas.tex: \text{kinematic: } \U \text{ imposed, } \partial_t\B = \nabla\times(\U\times\B) + \etaP\nabla^{2}\B \text{ is linear in } \B:\quad \B(\mathbf{x},t) = e^{s t}\,\hat{\B}(\mathbf{x}),\ \ s = \text{real growth rate (modes may also oscillate)}
\text{dynamic: the Lorentz force of } \B \text{ acts back on } \U \text{ and saturates the growth}

sentences.text: To test ideas, physicists need a {u}flow{/} simple enough to write on one line, yet able to make a dynamo.
One classic choice: the ABC flow.
It fills space with identical twisting rooms.
Three crossed winds make the fluid corkscrew: it spins around the direction it moves.
This box returns higher on our climb.

$\nabla\times\U = \U$ · it spins around its own direction of motion

formulas.tex: \nabla\times\U = \U \ \ (\text{Beltrami flow, maximal helicity; streamlines partly chaotic}),\qquad \text{periodic box } [0, 2\pi)^3,\ \ A = B = C = 1

sentences.text: Now turn one {param}knob{/} on this flow: Rm. Turning it up means less diffusion.
Less smudging should only help the stretching.
So once the dynamo switches on, it stays on. Right?
Here is the growth rate, computed at twenty-four settings.
Below about nine, every {b}field{/} fades. Then growth turns positive: the dynamo is on.
Near seventeen and a half, it switches off again.
Above about twenty-seven, it comes back.
Not one threshold, but windows: turning a knob further does not always help.
It agrees with published results. No machine learning yet: this only tests the solver.

scenes.title: A panel of knobs

sentences.text: Real dynamos have not one {param}knob{/}, but a panel.
How hard the metal is stirred; how well it conducts.
What the discs are made of: remember the iron.
How unequal their speeds are: that is when VKS flipped.
For DRESDYN, a precessing tank: how fast its axis turns.
Even the wall counts: in VKS simulations, changing only its magnetic condition raised the threshold by about forty percent.

scenes.title: A handful of dots

sentences.text: Every turbulent dynamo simulation in three dimensions is very costly.
So only a handful of knob settings get simulated.
Each one is a mountain of data: a single snapshot can weigh more than a gigabyte.
Each run holds only a few flips.
And between the dots, there is nothing at all.

cards.text: learn the whole family of fields, even at {param}knob settings{/} between the dots

sentences.text: Those gaps are where this film lives.
The study behind this film asks three things.
One: can a {model}machine{/} learn the whole family of fields, even at knob settings between the dots?
Two: can it respect each law where it holds, exactly in every field, or {metric}on average{/} over many fields?
Three: can it tell us {metric}how often{/} the field flips?
To find out, the study's plan climbs a staircase, from three numbers to the shapes of real experiments.
One honest note: this independent study is prospective, built on small experiments on an ordinary computer, and not endorsed by MilaDy, its partners or the supervisors.

scenes.title: Two whirlpools and a corridor

params.note: knob schedule and speeds are scene choices inside the known range of Gamma (0.80-1.00); the threshold window and the coefficients come from ctx.data.e1

sentences.text: Use two dials as a map: {b}quadrupole{/} across, {b}dipole{/} up.
With the knob low, the state circles in one whirlpool, and stays.
A mirror twin circles the mirror whirlpool: dipole down.
Each start is trapped. The dipole never changes sign.
Now turn {param}Gamma{/} up.
Just above zero point eight six, the whirlpools touch: a narrow corridor opens.
The state lingers on one side, then slips through. The {b}dipole{/} flips.
Nothing here is random. So, will the flips come like clockwork?
No. Long waits and short ones, irregularly.
The dipole's sign prints uneven stripes, like the seafloor.

labels: Will the flips come like clockwork?

sentences.text: Set {param}Gamma{/} at zero point nine, and launch two copies, one millionth apart.
We know the state to six decimals. Can we predict the date of the next flip?
At first, the copies move as one.
But their gap nearly triples every eleven time units.
After about a hundred and fifty, they disagree completely.
The average wait between crossings is longer: over two hundred.
Each extra decimal buys only about twenty-five more time units.
So the forecast fades before the average wait ends. Only the statistics survive.

labels: We know the state to six decimals. Can we predict the date of the next flip?
A · yes: the equations are exact
B · only a short way ahead

scenes.title: The long exposure

sentences.text: The path is lost, so leave the shutter open.
Each pass leaves a little light: a glow builds.
A copy started on the other side first paints the mirror image.
Given time, both paint the same glow.
Where does the {b}dipole{/} spend its time? Two humps, the same for both.
This reproducible glow is the stationary distribution.
Below the threshold, each start paints its own whirlpool.

scenes.title: The shoebox

sentences.text: Now film the trajectory, one frame every two time units.
Neighbouring frames look alike.
Cut the film into frames.
Drop them in a shoebox, shake, and throw away the timestamps.
Pour the box out: the frames redraw the same glow.
Each frame is a snapshot: three dial readings, nothing more.
It carries no timestamp and no time order.
Yet the shoebox, plus the equations, answers many questions.
Averages, energy budgets, even how often the dipole crosses zero.

scenes.title: Crowd laws

sentences.text: Pick one photo. Its three dial readings give its energy.
From that photo alone, the equations tell how fast its energy changes.
Drop one marble per photo at that value.
Some photos are gaining energy, others losing it. The pile spreads wide.
Yet its average sits at zero.
Energy in equals energy out, on average.
Like a bank account: over the years, income matches spending, yet each day gains or loses.
This is a {metric}law of the crowd{/}. It holds for the shoebox, not for each photo.

scenes.title: A toll counter without a clock

predict.title: PREDICT
predict.question: One photo, no clock: can it give a rate?

sentences.text: A puzzle. How many cars cross this line each hour?
No clock. Just one photo from above, where every speedometer can be read.
Can one photo, with no time in it, give you a rate?
It can. Draw a thin strip around the line.
A fast car spends little time inside, so catching one there counts for more.
Add up the speeds of the cars inside, and divide by the strip's width.
On average, that is how many cars cross per hour.

scenes.title: Rice for the dipole

sentences.text: Back to the shoebox. Spread its photos out by their {b}dipole{/} reading.
The line to cross is zero: draw a thin strip around it.
Each photo also needs a speedometer.
No clock required: the dipole's equation turns the photo's three dial readings into a speed.
Up or down, both count, so keep only its size.
Add the speeds inside the strip, then divide by its width and by the total number of photos.
Out comes the {metric}crossing rate{/}.
Shrink the strip to nothing, and for well-behaved systems the recipe is exact: Rice's formula.
The catch: few photos land in a thin strip. Here, about two dozen out of eight thousand.

labels: sum of speeds in the strip ÷ strip width ÷ total number of photos

formulas.tex: \ck{r_0} = \int |y|\,p_{D,\dot D}(0,y)\,dy = \lim_{h\to 0}\tfrac{1}{2h}\,\mathbb{E}\big[|\dot D|\,\mathbf{1}_{|D|<h}\big]\ \ \text{if } D \text{ is stationary, } C^1, \text{ and } (D,\dot D) \text{ has a continuous density}
\hat r_0 = \tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} |\dot D_i|\,\mathbf{1}_{|D_i|<h}/(2h),\ \ \dot D_i = -0.1\,D_i + V_i Q_i,\ \ h = 0.2;\ \ \text{bias } O(h^2),\ \text{variance } O(1/(Nh))

The two curves almost coincide.
Shade the gap, and divide by the area under the counted curve: the {metric}cumulative error{/}.
Four percent near the threshold, six percent above it.
A good sign, on three chaotic dials that are not even guaranteed to be well-behaved.

sentences.text: How is the wind learned? With a simple trick.
Keep one coordinate of each point, and lay the transport clock out to the right.
Pair each noise point with a random snapshot; join them with a straight string.
Thousands of strings, crossing everywhere.
Pick one place, at one moment.
Several strings pass through, pointing different ways.
The network learns one arrow there: their {model}average direction{/}.
That is the whole training: plain regression, like fitting a curve through points.
Follow the averaged wind, not the strings.
The paths bend, and drawn against the clock, they never cross.
Learn the average exactly, and the noise lands exactly on the data's crowd.

scenes.title: The noise floor

params.note: every quantity is a seeded illustration (a fair die, two sand piles): no number is shown, so no data file is needed

sentences.text: A generated snapshot has no true twin, so we compare crowds.
Picture each crowd as a pile of sand.
A {metric}distribution distance{/} scores how different the two piles are.
The earth-mover kind counts how much sand must move, and how far.
A perfect model, scored against the data: will it get zero?
No. Roll a fair die a thousand times, then a thousand more.
Same die, same truth, yet the two histograms differ.
That gap is the {metric}noise floor{/}, about what a perfect model scores.
Judge every model against it, at equal sample size, never against zero.
One catch: the samples must be independent.
Overlap them, and the floor drops too low, as the report warns.

labels: A perfect model, scored against the data: zero?

formulas.tex: \ck{\mathcal{E}}(P_1, P_2) = 2\,\mathbb{E}\|X - Y\| - \mathbb{E}\|X - X'\| - \mathbb{E}\|Y - Y'\|\ \ (= 0 \iff P_1 = P_2)

chips: technical names: energy distance (main score of E1 and E2) · Wasserstein W1, earth-mover (sliced in E1)
REFERENCE · Rubner, Tomasi & Guibas 2000 · Székely & Rizzo 2013

On 'overlap-0.15': the second die sample is rebuilt with params.overlap_share of its rolls copied from the first (those rolls flash in the first histogram, then reappear in the second, lighter shade): the two histograms come closer, and the dashed floor line in the bar chart slides DOWN, label 'overlapping samples: floor too low' with a pen arrow showing the drop; 1.5 s later the honest line returns to its first height with a pen check and the label 'independent samples: honest floor'. The dashed floor stays to the end (it returns in every results chart from ch07 on). scenes.title: A lopsided machine

sentences.text: Physics hands the machine two kinds of laws.
Some hold for every single snapshot.
Others hold only for the crowd.
Two shelves, still empty.
Back to the three dials, at a {param}Gamma{/} never seen in training.
Grey: true snapshots.
Violet: a plain {model}generator{/}.
The shape is right.
Now weigh the sides.
The truth is balanced; the machine is not.
Only about four in ten of its snapshots point up.
It copied its data: below the threshold, each run stays in one whirlpool, and the runs split unevenly.

sentences.text: Two ways to teach the mirror.
The first student, data augmentation, sees each training snapshot flipped half the time.
The second, equivariance, has the mirror built into its wind: a mirrored noise point always lands on the mirrored snapshot.
At a {param}Gamma{/} neither has seen, who stays balanced?
The built-in mirror.
The first student tilts a little.
Yet in the mirror's crowd, each snapshot still points one way.
The mirror balances the crowd, not each snapshot.
Its card goes on the crowd shelf: built in, exactly.

Below the threshold, runs often split unevenly: at zero point eight six, only five of sixteen runs point up.
The plain {model}machine{/} copies the imbalance, and spills it onto unseen settings.
Augmentation sits on the {metric}noise floor{/} at its training settings.
Between them, it drifts: the network fills the gaps freely.
The built-in mirror stays on the floor everywhere.
Flipped copies teach the mirror only where there are data.

scenes.title: Predict: balance every snapshot?

predict.title: PREDICT
predict.question: Force every snapshot to balance exactly: better or worse?

sentences.text: Remember the budget of the shoebox.
Snapshot by snapshot, energy rises or falls.
Only the crowd balances, on average, like a bank account over the years.
Now, a tempting fix for the machine.
Force every generated snapshot to balance its budget exactly. Better, or worse?
Worse.
Push each snapshot until its energy stops changing: the wide pile collapses into a spike at zero.
A ledger where every single day balances.
No real account looks like that.
The {metric}distribution distance{/} to the truth grows ninefold.
A short proof says why: even a perfect generator, forced this way, cannot match the truth.
So the budget goes on the crowd shelf.
On the next test bench, a cruder score is fooled by such a spike.

scenes.title: Enforce it on the crowd, with two juries

sentences.text: Impose the budget on the crowd, during training.
Draw a batch of snapshots at any {param}Gamma{/}, even without data.
Average their energy change and square it: this penalty, the crowd loss, vanishes only when the crowd balances.
But there is a trap.
Even for a balanced crowd, a batch's average wobbles; its square grows with the scatter.
So training also squeezes the scatter, nudging every snapshot toward balance: toward the spike.
It showed up while building this experiment.
The fix: split the batch into two independent juries and multiply their averages.
On average, the scatter drops out, leaving only the crowd's imbalance.
Does it pay off? The next tests will tell.

question.say: In three dimensions, which budgets should generated fields meet on average, and must their spread match too?
question.fr: En 3D, quels bilans les champs générés doivent-ils respecter en moyenne, et leur dispersion doit-elle aussi être celle des simulations ?
question.why: A budget forced on each field becomes a spike that a spectrum score misses (E2); even the crowd loss narrowed the spread by a quarter (E1). The 3D plan sets no such criterion, and the 3D evaluation logs mean residuals only.
question.unblocks: Which budgets the 3D crowd loss imposes (energy is coded; cross or magnetic helicity would need code), the spread metric to add to the 3D evaluation before renting, and that run's verdict rule.
question.why_fr: Un bilan imposé à chaque champ devient un pic qu'un score spectral ne voit pas (E2) ; même la perte en loi a resserré la dispersion d'un quart (E1). Le plan 3D ne fixe aucun critère de ce type, et l'évaluation 3D n'enregistre que des résidus moyens.
question.unblocks_fr: Les bilans qu'impose la perte en loi en 3D (l'énergie est codée ; l'hélicité croisée ou magnétique demanderait du code), la métrique de dispersion à ajouter à l'évaluation 3D avant de louer, et la règle de verdict de ce run.

sentences.text: First fix: draw a hill map, not arrows, and let the {u}flow{/} run along its contour lines.
Where the lines crowd, it runs faster, so nothing piles up or leaks, whatever the landscape.
The box agrees: lines in, lines out.
So the {model}machine{/} draws two hill maps, for the {u}flow{/} and the {b}field{/}: zero divergence by construction, however badly it is trained.
Second fix, for any field: split it into swirl plus slope, and delete the slope.
Wave by wave, remove the part of each arrow along the wave's own direction.
The gauges fall to rounding error, down to ten to the minus seventeen.
Measured, though, with the very operator used to enforce it.

scenes.title: Why almost is not exactly

params.note: a schematic illustration of Proposition 2 (c)-(d): no number on screen, no data file

sentences.text: Back to the plain {model}generator{/}: why does it miss, trained on clean data?
Follow the part of a field breaking the law.
To bring it exactly to zero, the {model}wind{/} must act as a spring that turns infinitely stiff as the transport clock runs out.
A bounded network cannot, and a sampler with finite steps cannot follow either.
A gap of order one remains: almost is not exactly.

labels: the part that breaks the law
needs infinite stiffness at the end
chips: SCHEMATIC · a spring, not the network
full statement: Proposition 2 and Remark 3.6 · extension X2.2

sentences.text: Now the crowd law: on average, energy in equals energy out.
Three ways to impose it, at settings of {param}eta{/} never seen.
One: during training, the crowd loss, with its two juries.
Against a control run of equal length, the {metric}distribution distance{/} drops from two point five to zero point seven.
The control itself gains nothing.
Two: after training, reweight the generated crowd.
Where the model is worst, a poll of five hundred shrinks to one person, and the crowd gets worse.
Three: rescale every snapshot onto the budget.
Each snapshot now dissipates the same: a spike, under a thousandth of the true spread.
Yet the same {metric}distribution distance{/}, built on spectra, improves: it is fooled.
Only the spread gives the spike away. The crowd loss shows no spike.
One training seed each, interpolation only, every model far above the noise floor.

sentences.text: Back to the two shelves, now full.
For every snapshot: zero divergence. Build it in, or project, and it holds exactly; a penalty only roughly.
For the crowd: the energy budget. Impose it on the crowd during training. Reweighting afterwards fails where the model is poor; forcing it onto each snapshot makes a spike.
And the mirror? Each snapshot is lopsided, so it is a crowd law, yet a network can carry it exactly, built in.
One rule sorts them all: enforce each law where it is true.

sentences.text: Put the pieces together: the machine this study proposes.
A {model}wind{/} carries noise to a symmetric crowd of codes, mirror built in.
A decoder turns each code into hill maps, so every field is divergence-free.
And the energy budget is imposed on the crowd.
It has not been built as a whole: the experiments tested pieces, on three dials and a flat sheet, with small networks on an ordinary processor.
One question remains: from snapshots, how well can we answer {metric}how often{/}?

question.en: In the partners' solver snapshots, which laws hold *exactly*, and under which *discrete operator*?
question.say: In the partners' solver snapshots, which laws hold exactly, and under which discrete operator?
question.fr: Dans les instantanés des codes du consortium, SFEMaNS et LATU, quelles lois valent exactement, et pour quel opérateur discret ?
question.why: Exact laws are built into the decoder, but exact depends on the operator: SFEMaNS controls ∇·B only weakly, so a generator would be more solenoidal than its data.
question.unblocks: What the decoder builds in (divergence, wall and interface conditions), the operator that measures divergence, and what each stored snapshot must carry to recompute it.
question.why_fr: Les lois exactes s'intègrent au décodeur, mais « exact » dépend de l'opérateur : SFEMaNS ne contrôle ∇·B que faiblement, si bien qu'un générateur serait plus solénoïdal que ses données.
question.unblocks_fr: Ce que le décodeur intègre par construction (divergence, conditions aux parois et aux interfaces), l'opérateur qui mesure la divergence, et ce que chaque instantané stocké doit contenir pour la recalculer.

sentences.text: The toll counter is back: every car is now {model}generated{/}.
They come from the machine with the built-in mirror: twenty thousand at each of forty-one settings of {param}Gamma{/}, most unseen in training.
Rice, with the equations, turns them into a {metric}crossing rate{/}.
Against the counted truth, far from the threshold, the {metric}cumulative error{/} is fourteen percent.
Setting by setting, the miss averages seventeen percent, and reaches sixty-five percent at two settings.
Near the threshold, the error climbs to forty-two percent.
One model, one training seed.
Rice needs the equations, and gives a rate, not waiting times.
So, the study's third question: can a machine tell us {metric}how often{/}?
For crossings on three dials: far from the threshold, roughly yes; near it, not yet.

scenes.title: Predict: early, late or on time?

badge.note: E1 · fine grid · model C, seed 0

predict.title: PREDICT
predict.question: Near the threshold, will the generated rate switch on early, late, or on time?

sentences.text: Zoom in. The truth is silent up to zero point eight six.
But the machine changes smoothly with {param}Gamma{/}.
Will its crossing rate switch on early, late, or on time?
Early and late, but never on time.
Below the threshold, it leaks false crossings: up to a tenth of the rate just above.
At zero point eight six five, it is late: less than a sixth of the counted rate.
Just above, it overshoots: five crossings per thousand time units, against three point four.

labels: Near the threshold, will the generated rate switch on early, late, or on time?
onset late by about 0.005-0.01 in Γ

scenes.title: A stiff sheet on a steep ramp

badge.note: Prop. 9, a lower bound · E1 consistent with it, seed 0

metaphor.ramp_from: sweep.bridge_fine.reference (monotone envelope of the fine-grid bridge mass)

sentences.text: Why? Picture the machine as a stiff sheet: as {param}Gamma{/} turns, its crowd changes only so fast.
The truth climbs a steep ramp: just above zero point eight six, the corridor opens.
The sheet rounds the corner: too early, then too low.
The data show both: early strays in the corridor, then too few at the threshold.
A theorem: at a true jump, a smooth machine misses by at least half of it.
Unless it is very supple, or told which state the system is in.
Here, a ramp, not a jump, and one seed: consistent with the theorem, not proof.
Nor does the theorem explain the overshoot.

labels: unless: very supple, or told which state
chips: SCHEMATIC · stiff sheet and cliff (shape only)
consistent with Prop. 9 · one model, seed 0

scenes.visual: Render class dense2d (two Canvas point clouds; each of the 21 frames per cloud is rasterized once in setup into an offscreen canvas, per frame only the visible index and opacities change; the metaphor and the curves are SVG). Key colours: green (knob, Γ axis), violet (the sheet, the generated cloud), amber (bridge-mass curves, the corridor band); the reference cloud is --silver with the white SIMULATED chip. No corner needle (snapshots, as in 04.6). Pictures first, words after, formula last (B3, styles 3.7). P1, the metaphor (SCHEMATIC chip, grey dashed, bottom-left of the metaphor box). On 'sheet-0.15': in params.metaphor.box a side view: a green Γ axis (no numbers but a tick at 0.86); a violet translucent sheet (params.metaphor.sheet: a thick ribbon seen edge-on, --model at 35 % with a 2-px violet top edge) drops from above and settles flat; a small green knob (M2) under the axis turns and the sheet shifts only slowly, as if hinged on springs (its curvature is capped: label 'the machine: a stiff sheet'). On 'ramp-0.15': the TRUE ramp draws on under it in amber (solid 4 px): flat at zero, then a steep rise just above the 0.86 tick (shape: monotone envelope of sweep.bridge_fine.reference, normalized to the box; no y numbers here), label 'truth: a steep ramp'; a short squeal (sfx, -30 dB, the 01.3 threshold callback) as the ramp bends. On 'round-0.15': the sheet sags onto the ramp and settles as the closed-form minimizer of misfit + stiffness x curvature (a cubic smoothing spline of the ramp with params.metaphor.sheet.stiffness, computed in setup, no physics engine): it lifts before the knee and stays under the ramp after it; the pen labels the two gaps 'too early' (left of the knee) and 'too low' (right of it). The sheet must not overshoot in the metaphor: the bound does not explain the overshoot (critique A5). P2, the data. On 'clouds-0.15': the metaphor slides left and shrinks to 60 %; at the right, two square cloud panels (params.clouds.boxes; Q across, D up, range ±2.4, no tick labels, axis names 'Q' and 'D' in 28 px): 'reference' (--silver points, SIMULATED chip) and 'generated · model C, seed 0' (violet points, violet frame, GENERATED chip); a horizontal amber band |D| < 0.25 across both (label 'the corridor · |D| < 0.25'); points inside the band are drawn larger (params.clouds.bridge_point_px) in amber with a violet or silver rim. The knob (params.knob) steps through the 21 values of sweep.gammas, both clouds switching frame by frame: SLOWLY over 0.80-0.86 (params.clouds.dwell_below_s each, a soft detent sfx at the first step only), where the reference band stays empty while single stray generated points sit in it (1 of 4,000 at 0.80, 0.82, 0.84 and 0.85; the pen rings each one as it appears), then QUICKLY above (params.clouds.dwell_above_s each), where both bands fill. The clouds carry the LEAK only: with 4,000 points and no cloud at 0.865 (not a data Γ), they cannot resolve the lag, and at 0.87 the small cloud even shows the opposite (6 of 4,000 against 0.11 % for the reference): do not dwell above 0.86. The LAG is read on the fine-grid curve: simultaneously the metaphor box morphs (T1) into the bridge-mass chart (params.bridge_plot): reference curve from e1.bridge.reference (solid amber) and generated curve from e1.bridge.model_C (amber DASHED, violet chip GENERATED; 41 Γ, 20,000 generated per Γ), drawn on left to right in step with the knob; at the words 'too few at the threshold' the pen draws a short brace at 0.865 between the two curves (0.00025 generated against 0.00167); the stiff-sheet ribbon fades to a 20 % ghost around the dashed curve. Chip 'clouds: 4,000 generated per Γ · curve: 20,000' small under the clouds (honest about the two sample sizes). P3, the bound, picture first. On 'bound-0.15': the chart dims to 40 %; in its place a cliff ghost (params.metaphor.cliff_ghost: the ramp replaced by a vertical step, grey dashed) with the violet sheet crossing it at mid-height; the pen (M9) draws a brace on the full step, label 'jump', then a brace from the sheet to the step's far side, label 'miss ≥ about half the jump'; on 'unless-0.15', chalk text 'unless: very supple, or told which state' (a supple sheet = a large K; 'which state' = conditioning on the state or branch label, hysteresis, R:557, T:913; 'branch' itself is not introduced in the core cut, so it is not used here) The formula layer shows Proposition 9 from 'sheet' (Lipschitz in Γ) and from 'bound' (the inequality), 'Formula · R:544-557'. On 'honest-0.15': the cliff ghost melts back into the steep ramp (T6-like morph, 0.8 s); the chart returns to full opacity and the caption 'leaks · lags · overshoots' of 09.2 writes on under it; then, on 'overshoot-0.15', the pen crosses out nothing but circles the overshoot hump at 0.875-0.885 with a dotted (not solid) circle and a small grey question mark: the bound does not explain it; plain chip 'consistent with Prop. 9 · one model, seed 0' top-right under the badge. Badge PROVED (note 'Prop. 9, a lower bound · E1 consistent with it, seed 0'). sentences.text: The scoreboard: eight mechanisms, each with a verdict.
For every snapshot: hill maps and projection, exact; the penalty, approximate.
For the crowd: the mirror, exact; the crowd loss, useful but not clean; the rest, failures.
Back to the study's three questions.
One: between the dots, the shapes come out right, but no model reaches its {metric}noise floor{/}.
Two: each law where it holds, exactly yes, {metric}on average{/} partly.
Three, {metric}how often{/}: roughly right far from the threshold, poor near it.
Three lessons.
Exact laws: build them in.
Crowd laws: impose them on the crowd, never on each snapshot.
And judge every result against the noise floor, with enough seeds.

question.en: Which settings should get runs long enough to *count* reversals, so a predicted rate can be *checked*?
question.say: Which settings should get runs long enough to count reversals, so a predicted rate can be checked?
question.fr: Pour quels réglages faut-il des simulations assez longues pour *compter* les renversements, afin de *vérifier* un taux prédit ?
question.why: A predicted rate is only checked against a count: E1 counted 93 to 572 crossings per setting. The reversal simulations hold few reversals, and the configured Taylor–Green runs keep 40 time units.
question.unblocks: Run length and trajectories per setting (t_keep, n_traj), which settings get long runs and which only snapshots, and the error bar a rate is judged by (5 % or a Poisson interval).
question.why_fr: Un taux prédit ne se vérifie que contre un comptage : E1 a compté de 93 à 572 passages par réglage. Les simulations de renversements en contiennent peu, et les simulations Taylor–Green configurées ne gardent que 40 unités de temps.
question.unblocks_fr: La durée et le nombre de trajectoires par réglage (t_keep, n_traj), les réglages qui reçoivent de longues simulations et ceux qui ne fournissent que des instantanés, et la barre d'erreur qui juge un taux (5 % ou un intervalle de Poisson).

Some carry the equations in their loss; others learn maps between whole fields.
For conducting fluids, they now reach flat, two-dimensional turbulence.

Their weak spot: trained to minimize a mean-square error, ensembles of them regress to the mean flow.
A cloud with two polarities collapses to its middle.

sentences.text: Third track: making samples obey the laws. Four families.
Hard: build the law into the network, say a potential whose curl has no divergence, or project each sample while drawing it.
Soft: a penalty in the loss, obeyed only approximately.
On the {metric}distribution{/}: constrain the crowd, by its covariance, or by the equation a steady cloud obeys.
And symmetry: an equivariant flow gives a symmetric cloud.
A twenty twenty-six preprint compared ways to impose zero divergence on flat flows: no single strategy dominates.
In three dimensions, we found two exactly divergence-free generators, both preprints: periodic-box turbulence, and a current-free field in the Sun's corona.
None handles walls, a vacuum outside and iron inside.

sentences.text: Now the rings: papers co-signed by the supervisors.
Dynamo side: Taylor–Green dynamos pushed to small {param}magnetic Prandtl numbers{/}, and the VKS tank with its iron impellers, simulated in two codes.
In twenty twenty-six, both codes produced VKS reversals, and a four-dial model reproduces their main features.
Learning side: autoencoder latent spaces read through classical flow modes, von Kármán flow included.
And assimilation and diffusion models built on deep networks, outside conducting fluids.
Three ingredients are in hand. But in what we found, none of the four has published a {model}generative model{/} trained on dynamo data.

sentences.text: Where the {model}generative{/} and constraint tracks cross the dynamo tracks, we found the map empty.
An independent thesis proposal aims at that spot: five gaps, each beside its nearest neighbour.
One: a generator of dynamo fields.
Two: {u}velocity{/} and {b}magnetic field{/} with exactly zero divergence, in a walled cylinder with iron and vacuum.
Three: energy budgets imposed on the {metric}distribution{/}, with no target value, even where there are no data.
Four: the flip rate read from snapshots with Rice's formula.
Five: one generator that crosses the dynamo threshold.
The study tested pieces on toy cases: exact potentials on a flat sheet, a budget imposed without data, Rice's formula on three dials.

question.en: First VKS data: should the generator train on *LATU*'s periodic grid or *SFEMaNS*'s cylinder mesh?
question.say: First VKS data: should the generator train on the LATU periodic grid, or the SFEMaNS cylinder mesh?
question.fr: Premières données VKS : le générateur doit-il s'entraîner sur la grille périodique de *LATU* ou sur le maillage cylindrique de *SFEMaNS* ?
question.why: Both codes produce reversals in simulated VKS (Bousquet et al. 2026). LATU gives pseudo-spectral fields in a periodic (3π)³ box, cylinder and impellers imposed by penalization: the periodic route to exact zero divergence applies there (T:111), though the Fourier basis of E2 alone no longer suffices (R:1185). SFEMaNS gives azimuthal Fourier modes on a meridian finite-element mesh, with iron and a vacuum potential, and controls ∇·B only weakly (R:1185): the setting no generator found handles (gap 2).
question.unblocks: Which data reader and decoder are written first (T:1028); whether tier 3 can start at month 15 on the periodic decoder while the hybrid decoder, vacuum matching and iron kink are built (E:496); and which solver's snapshots the first data request names (R:1209).
question.why_fr: Les deux codes produisent des renversements dans VKS simulé (Bousquet et al. 2026). LATU fournit des champs pseudo-spectraux dans une boîte périodique (3π)³, cylindre et turbines imposés par pénalisation : la voie périodique vers une divergence exactement nulle s'y applique (T:111), même si la base de Fourier de E2 ne suffit plus (R:1185). SFEMaNS fournit des modes de Fourier azimutaux sur un maillage méridien d'éléments finis, avec du fer et un potentiel dans le vide, et ne contrôle ∇·B que faiblement (R:1185) : le cas qu'aucun générateur trouvé ne traite (lacune 2).
question.unblocks_fr: Le lecteur de données et le décodeur à écrire d'abord (T:1028) ; la possibilité de lancer le palier 3 au mois 15 avec le décodeur périodique pendant que le décodeur hybride, le raccord au vide et le pli à l'interface du fer sont construits (E:496) ; et le solveur dont la première demande de données nomme les instantanés (R:1209).

scenes.title: Walls and iron

iron.kink_profile: potential across the interface: smooth (C1) vs kinked (|d|)

sentences.text: Leave the periodic box for a real vessel, and exact gets harder.
The potential needs a gauge and a wall condition; then each {b}field{/} has exactly one.
At the soft-iron impellers, {b}field lines{/} bend sharply at the iron's surface, so a smooth potential cannot be exact: it needs a kink there.
Outside, the {b}field{/} must match a current-free field in the vacuum.
The rule is linear but nonlocal: the {b}field{/} at one point of the wall depends on the whole wall.
Imposing it exactly and cheaply, for every sample, is still open.

labels: gauge + wall condition → one potential per field
one point depends on the whole wall

sentences.text: Back to the compass, and to the two questions.
When will this needle turn?
For the Earth, no one can say.
In a simple computer model, chaos makes the forecast fade before the average wait ends.
But {metric}how often{/} the field flips, counted as crossings of zero, can still be answered.
The answer hides in a shoebox of snapshots, read with the equations.
And a {model}machine{/} can learn to dream such snapshots, between the simulated settings.
On small test problems, it partly works.
The mirror holds by construction, at every setting.
On three dials, the {metric}rate of zero crossings{/} is roughly right far from the threshold, and poor near it.
A smooth machine rounds off a steep change.
The bigger tests, in three dimensions and in the shapes of real machines, are written as bets.
One lesson remains.
Enforce each law where it is true.
Exactly, where it is exact.
{metric}On average{/}, where it only holds on average.

labels: Enforce each law where it is true.
On average, where it only holds on average.

The internship report is prospective: the internship has not taken place, and its results come from small experiments run on an ordinary processor, reproducible from the repository. No MilaDy consortium data were used. Nothing here was reviewed, discussed or validated by Sibo Cheng, Didier Lucor, Caroline Nore or Yannick Ponty, and no sentence expresses their opinion. The PhD topic is an independent proposal, neither requested nor validated by them.
